questions.stem: Which property certifies that a greedy choice is safe?
choices: It runs in O(n log n) time
An optimal solution can be transformed via an exchange to contain the greedy choice without worsening the objective
questions.explanation: Greedy safety is established by an exchange argument: any optimal solution can be modified to include the greedy choice without harming the objective.

questions.stem: Which greedy rule is optimal for unweighted Interval Scheduling?
questions.explanation: Earliest Finish Time leaves the most resource available for later jobs. The other three rules each have simple counter-examples.

questions.stem: For Fractional Knapsack, which sort key gives an optimal greedy?
questions.explanation: Sort by b_i / w_i descending and pack greedily. Exchange argument: moving weight from a low-ratio item to a higher-ratio item strictly improves the objective.

questions.stem: Why does the ratio-greedy fail for 0/1 Knapsack?
choices: Items cannot be split, so a high-ratio item that doesn't fit cannot be replaced by partial pieces, breaking the exchange
questions.explanation: Without fractional pieces the exchange argument fails — you cannot move arbitrary amounts of weight between items. 0/1 Knapsack is NP-complete.

questions.stem: In the Minimising Lateness problem, what is an 'inversion'?
choices: A pair of jobs with equal deadlines
A pair (i, k) scheduled in the order k, i but with d_i < d_k
A job whose lateness exceeds its length
Any job that finishes after its deadline
questions.explanation: An inversion is two jobs out of deadline order in the schedule. EDF has no inversions, and swapping adjacent inversions never increases max lateness.

questions.stem: What is the running time of the standard EDF / EFT / fractional-knapsack greedy algorithms?
questions.explanation: Sorting dominates; the sweep is linear. So O(n log n) overall.

questions.stem: What is the 'depth' of an interval instance in Interval Partitioning?
choices: Maximum number of intervals overlapping any single point in time
questions.explanation: Depth is the max point-overlap. It is a structural lower bound on the number of rooms needed, and greedy by start-time achieves it.

questions.stem: Which technique proves Interval Partitioning greedy is optimal?
questions.explanation: Any partition needs >= depth rooms (lower bound). The greedy never opens more than depth rooms (upper bound). Together they imply optimality.

questions.stem: Which counter-example shows that 'shortest interval' is NOT optimal for Interval Scheduling?
choices: Three intervals all of equal length
A short interval that overlaps two disjoint longer intervals
questions.explanation: If a 1-unit interval overlaps two non-overlapping 10-unit intervals, taking the short one yields 1 job; taking the two long ones yields 2.

questions.stem: When proving EDF optimal via exchange, what is shown about swapping an adjacent inversion?
choices: It does not increase max lateness
It changes the deadlines of both jobs
questions.explanation: The swap may keep max lateness the same or decrease it; the proof only needs 'does not increase'. Iterating turns any schedule into EDF.

questions.stem: Which problem from this week is solved by a structural lower bound rather than an exchange argument?
questions.explanation: Interval Partitioning's proof matches greedy's room count to the depth lower bound. The others use exchange / stays-ahead arguments.

questions.stem: Which is the right next step if your first greedy heuristic seems to work?
choices: Stress-test against small counter-examples; if it survives, prove correctness
Skip the proof and benchmark on random inputs
questions.explanation: Most natural heuristics fail. Construct adversarial small inputs first; only then attempt a proof.

questions.stem: In a 'stays ahead' proof, what is the inductive claim?
choices: Greedy is always strictly faster than OPT
Greedy's k-th element finishes no later than OPT's k-th element
Greedy's solution contains OPT as a subset
OPT and greedy have the same final element
questions.explanation: You show greedy's k-th finish time is <= OPT's k-th finish time for every k. This is how Interval Scheduling correctness is proved.

questions.stem: In Fractional Knapsack, what is the time complexity of computing the optimal value?
questions.explanation: Sort by ratio (O(n log n)) and sweep once. There is no W-dependent term.

questions.stem: Which problem does NOT admit an optimal greedy algorithm?
questions.explanation: 0/1 Knapsack is NP-complete and requires DP (O(nW)) in general. The others have known optimal greedy rules.

questions.stem: Why does sorting by deadline (EDF) make the exchange argument easy for Minimising Lateness?
choices: Adjacent jobs in EDF are by definition not inverted, so the proof reduces to showing each adjacent swap is safe
It removes ties from the schedule
questions.explanation: EDF is precisely the inversion-free schedule, so showing 'remove adjacent inversion does not increase lateness' implies EDF is optimal.

questions.stem: Which sort key powers the optimal Interval Partitioning greedy?
questions.explanation: Sort intervals by start time; assign to the lowest-numbered compatible room (or open a new one). This achieves the depth lower bound.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a correct general 'recipe' for designing a greedy algorithm?
choices: Define the greedy rule, then test on small inputs
Find a sort key that captures local optimality
Prove correctness via exchange or structural argument
questions.explanation: Overlapping subproblems is the DP signature. Greedy does not memoise — it commits irrevocably to one choice.

questions.stem: Suppose intervals have varying weights and you want max total weight of a disjoint subset. Does Earliest Finish Time still work?
choices: Yes; it always works for interval problems
No; weighted interval scheduling needs dynamic programming
Only if weights are all equal
questions.explanation: Weighted Interval Scheduling defeats greedy in general — a single high-weight long interval can outweigh many short ones. Week 4 solves it with O(n log n) DP.

questions.stem: What is the correctness lemma used in the Earliest Finish Time proof?
questions.explanation: Stays-ahead: by induction, greedy's k-th finish time is no later than OPT's k-th. Hence greedy can keep selecting at least as long, so |G| >= |OPT|.

questions.stem: Which best describes a counter-example you should reach for when sanity-checking a greedy rule?
choices: A small (3-5 item) hand-built adversarial input where greedy and OPT disagree
questions.explanation: Adversarial 3-5 item inputs are the cheapest way to refute a candidate greedy. Random or large inputs hide subtle failures.

questions.stem: In Minimising Lateness with EDF, what time does the optimal max lateness equal in the worst case?
choices: max_j (sum of t_i over earlier-deadline jobs + t_j - d_j) clipped at zero
Always equal to total processing time
questions.explanation: After EDF the lateness of each job is determined by accumulated processing time; the max lateness has the form given. It is not always zero.

questions.stem: Why does greedy run after a sort, rather than before?
choices: The sort imposes the order in which the greedy rule is applied; without it the rule is meaningless
Sorting reduces the number of items
questions.explanation: The local 'best' is defined by the sort key. Greedy is precisely 'sweep in sort order, take each item if feasible'.

questions.stem: An exchange argument typically transforms OPT into greedy in how many steps?
choices: At most a polynomial number of objective-preserving swaps
questions.explanation: Iterated polynomially many local swaps, each preserving (or improving) the objective, converts OPT into greedy. The argument implies greedy is optimal.

questions.stem: Which problem is solved by 'least busy room' assignment in greedy order?
questions.explanation: Interval Partitioning sorts by start time and assigns each interval to the lowest-indexed free room, opening a new room only when forced.
